### 3-Layer Torch-Down Flat Roof Replacement

Source: https://roof-ex.com/blog/field-notes/3-layer-torch-down-flat-roof-replacement

3-Layer Torch-Down Flat Roof Replacement

A Complete Modified Bitumen Roofing System
When a flat or low-slope roof begins leaking, developing bubbles, separating at seams, holding water, or showing widespread deterioration, repeated patching may no longer be the best long-term solution.

A complete flat roof replacement with a 3-layer torch-down modified bitumen roofing system can provide a durable, multi-layer waterproofing system designed specifically for low-slope roofing applications.

Roof Express recently completed this type of roofing system using a comprehensive approach that addresses much more than the visible surface of the roof.

From tear-off and roof-deck inspection to new flashing, waterproofing, drainage details, and the final granulated cap sheet, each component plays an important role in the performance of the completed roof.

In this article, we'll explain what a 3-layer torch-down roof is, how the system is built, why it is commonly used on flat roofs, and what homeowners should expect from a professional flat roof replacement.
What Is a 3-Layer Torch-Down Roof?
A 3-layer torch-down roof is a multi-ply modified bitumen roofing system designed for flat and low-slope roofs.

A typical three-ply assembly can include:

Layer 1 — Base Sheet

Layer 2 — Modified Bitumen Interply or Smooth Membrane

Layer 3 — Granulated Modified Bitumen Cap Sheet

GAF, for example, publishes three-ply APP modified-bitumen assemblies consisting of a base sheet, interply, and cap membrane.

Together, these layers create a reinforced roofing assembly rather than relying on a single membrane for waterproofing.

The exact products and attachment methods should always be selected according to the roof design, substrate, manufacturer requirements, applicable building codes, and project conditions.
Why Use Modified Bitumen on a Flat Roof?
Flat and low-slope roofs behave differently from steep pitched roofs.

On a steep roof, gravity moves rainwater toward the gutters relatively quickly.

On a low-slope roof, water drains more slowly. That makes waterproofing, seams, flashing, penetrations, and drainage especially important.

Modified bitumen roofing systems are specifically designed for low-slope applications. Manufacturers including CertainTeed and GAF identify modified-bitumen systems as options for residential and commercial low-slope roofing.

A properly selected multi-layer modified bitumen system can provide:

Strong waterproofing

Multiple layers of protection

Reinforced roofing membranes

Resistance to normal roof movement

Protection against sun and weather exposure

Durable seams

Protection around penetrations

A finished granulated surface

Long-term performance when correctly installed and maintained

Our Flat Roof Replacement Process
A quality flat roof replacement starts long before the final cap sheet is installed.

The condition underneath the existing roofing is equally important.

Here is how a professional 3-layer torch-down roof replacement is approached.
1. Existing Flat Roof Inspection
Before beginning the project, the existing roofing system should be carefully evaluated.

The inspection may identify problems including:

Active roof leaks

Open seams

Bubbles or blisters

Cracked roofing membranes

Ponding water

Failed flashing

Deteriorated roof edges

Damaged drain areas

Previous roofing patches

Soft roof decking

Deterioration around skylights

Problems around plumbing vents

Roof-to-wall leakage

Understanding the existing problems helps determine the appropriate replacement scope.
2. Complete Tear-Off of Existing Roofing
For a complete roof replacement, the deteriorated roofing materials are removed from the areas included in the project.

A tear-off may include removing:

Existing roofing membranes

Old cap sheets

Underlying roofing layers

Loose roofing materials

Deteriorated flashing

Damaged accessories

Roofing debris

Removing the old roof exposes the underlying deck so its condition can be evaluated.

This is one of the biggest advantages of a complete tear-off compared with simply installing another roofing layer over an unknown substrate.
3. Roof Deck Inspection
Once the existing roofing is removed, the roof deck becomes visible.

The decking is inspected for conditions such as:

Rotten plywood

Water damage

Delamination

Soft areas

Previous improper repairs

Dry rot

Damaged wood

Structural concerns

A new roofing system performs best when installed over a sound and properly prepared substrate.

Installing premium roofing over severely deteriorated decking does not correct the underlying problem.
4. Replacement of Deteriorated Roof Decking
Any roof-deck areas requiring replacement should be addressed before installing the new waterproofing system.

This may involve removing deteriorated sheathing and replacing it with suitable new roof decking.

Once repairs are completed, the contractor has a solid substrate for installation of the new roofing assembly.
5. Drainage and Ponding Evaluation
Drainage is one of the most important considerations on any flat roof.

Before installing the new roofing system, existing drainage conditions should be evaluated.

Water should be directed toward designated drainage points such as:

Roof drains

Scuppers

Gutters

Downspouts

Minor temporary water accumulation immediately following rain can occur on some low-slope roofs, but significant or persistent ponding should be evaluated.

When necessary and included in the project scope, drainage improvements may involve corrections to the substrate, tapered materials, crickets, framing, or other modifications.

The objective is not only to install new roofing but also to provide the best practical water-management system for the existing building.
6. Installation of the First Layer — Base Sheet
The first component of the new roofing assembly is the base sheet.

The base sheet creates the foundation for the modified bitumen roofing system and separates the finished membranes from the underlying roof deck or approved substrate.

The specific type of base sheet and attachment method depend on the roofing manufacturer, substrate, roof design, and selected system.

This first layer is extremely important because every additional membrane depends on the preparation underneath it.
7. Installation of the Second Layer — Modified Bitumen Interply
The second roofing layer provides another reinforced waterproofing membrane.

This layer may be referred to as the:

Interply

Ply sheet

Smooth modified bitumen membrane

Intermediate membrane

depending on the manufacturer and roofing system.

Adding an intermediate layer gives the roofing assembly additional redundancy.

Instead of depending on one finished membrane alone, a 3-ply system provides multiple layers between the building and outside weather.
8. Installation of the Third Layer — Granulated Cap Sheet
The final roofing layer is typically the granulated modified bitumen cap sheet.

The cap sheet forms the visible finished surface of the roof.

Its granulated surface helps protect the modified bitumen membrane against exposure while creating a durable finished roofing surface.

This final layer must be carefully integrated with:

Roof edges

Drains

Scuppers

Flashing

Plumbing vents

Skylights

Walls

Other roof penetrations

The performance of a flat roof depends heavily on these details.
Why Three Layers Instead of One?
One of the biggest advantages of a multi-ply roofing system is redundancy.

A 3-layer modified bitumen system does not rely solely on one membrane.

The complete assembly provides:

Base Sheet + Interply + Cap Sheet

Each layer performs a different function within the roofing system.

The result is a robust roofing assembly designed for low-slope environments where water moves more slowly than it does on a pitched roof.

Multi-ply modified-bitumen construction is recognized by roofing manufacturers as an established low-slope roofing approach.
Torch-Down Roofing and Waterproof Seams
Torch-applied modified bitumen uses heat during professional installation to bond compatible membrane layers together.

When installed according to the roofing manufacturer's specifications, the process creates tightly bonded membrane seams designed to resist water intrusion. GAF describes torch-down installation as heating modified-bitumen membrane so it bonds to the layer beneath.

Because torch-applied roofing involves open-flame equipment and specialized procedures, installation should be handled by trained roofing professionals following manufacturer requirements and appropriate fire-safety procedures.
Flashing Is Just as Important as the Roofing Membrane
A flat roof can contain excellent roofing material and still leak if the flashing details are poorly installed.

Many roof leaks begin at transitions rather than in the middle of the membrane.

Important areas include:

Roof-to-wall connections

Parapet walls

Skylights

Chimneys

Plumbing vents

Roof drains

Scuppers

HVAC penetrations

Electrical penetrations

Roof edges

Transitions between flat and pitched roofs

These areas require careful waterproofing and integration with the new roofing system.
Roof Drains and Scuppers
Water management is especially important on a flat roof.

Drain and scupper areas should be inspected as part of the reroofing process.

Common drainage problems include:

Clogged drains

Deteriorated drain flashing

Damaged drain components

Improper slope toward the drain

Debris accumulation

Water backing up at walls

Undersized or poorly located drainage points

A beautiful new roofing membrane will not perform at its best if the drainage system is ignored.
Skylights on Flat Roofs
Many flat roofs contain skylights.

These can become common leak locations when old flashing, deteriorated curbs, sealants, or surrounding roofing begins to fail.

During a flat roof replacement, skylights should be inspected for:

Deteriorated curb framing

Rotted wood

Damaged glazing

Failed seals

Corrosion

Previous repairs

Interior moisture staining

Deteriorated flashing

If an older skylight is already near the end of its service life, replacing it during the roofing project can make sense.

This allows the new skylight and new roofing system to be integrated together from the beginning.
Flat Roof Penetrations
Every penetration through the roof creates a potential waterproofing challenge.

Common flat-roof penetrations include:

Plumbing pipes

Exhaust vents

Electrical conduits

HVAC equipment

Skylights

Roof drains

Solar equipment

Chimneys

Each penetration must be properly incorporated into the roofing and flashing system.

Applying roofing cement around an old penetration should not be considered a substitute for properly designed flashing when replacement is required.
Roof-to-Wall Connections
Roof-to-wall transitions deserve special attention.

These locations commonly experience water intrusion because runoff can become concentrated along the wall.

Depending on the structure, waterproofing may involve properly integrated flashing, membrane upturns, counterflashing, siding coordination, or other system-specific details.

The exact design depends on the building and existing construction.
Granulated Cap Sheet Finish
Once the final cap sheet is installed, the roof has a clean and uniform finished surface.

Granulated cap sheets are popular because they combine the waterproofing characteristics of modified bitumen with a protective finished surface.

Depending on the selected roofing system, different cap-sheet colors or reflective surfaces may also be available.

Product selection should be based on manufacturer requirements and any applicable energy-code requirements.
Final Roof Inspection
After the roofing installation is completed, the finished system should be carefully reviewed.

The final inspection should include checking major roofing details such as:

Membrane surface

Seams

Roof edges

Flashing

Penetrations

Drain areas

Scuppers

Skylights

Roof-to-wall transitions

Finished waterproofing details

The roof and surrounding work areas should also be cleaned of construction debris.

Where a permit is required, applicable building inspections should also be completed.
Benefits of a 3-Layer Torch-Down Flat Roof
A professionally installed 3-layer modified bitumen roofing system offers several potential benefits.
Multi-Layer Protection
Three roofing plies provide redundancy rather than relying on one membrane.
Excellent Low-Slope Application
Modified bitumen is designed for flat and low-slope roofing applications.
Strong Waterproofing
Properly installed membrane systems create continuous waterproof roofing coverage.
Reinforced Roofing
Modified bitumen membranes incorporate reinforcing materials designed to improve strength and durability.
Resistance to Normal Building Movement

Durable Finished Surface
The granulated cap sheet provides a protective finished roofing surface.
Multiple Flashing Options
The system can be professionally detailed around many common flat-roof penetrations and transitions.

Existing roofing

Roof deck

Building occupancy

Fire-safety requirements

Drainage

Building code

Nearby combustible materials

Project design

You should consider a professional roof evaluation when you notice:

Recurring leaks

However, continuing to patch a roof that is failing throughout can become increasingly expensive.
Flat Roof Repair vs. Complete Replacement
A professional roofing contractor should evaluate whether repair or complete replacement makes more sense.
A Repair May Be Appropriate When:

Damage is isolated

The roofing system is relatively young

The surrounding membrane remains in good condition

Complete Replacement May Be Better When:

Leaks occur in multiple areas

Numerous previous repairs exist

Moisture has reached the roof deck

Seams are failing in multiple locations

The roof has reached the later stages of its useful life

Repair costs continue increasing

The goal should be to solve the roofing problem, not simply cover the visible symptom.

Frequently Asked Questions About 3-Layer Torch-Down RoofingWhat is a 3-layer torch-down roof?
A three-layer system typically consists of a base sheet, an intermediate modified-bitumen ply, and a finished modified-bitumen cap sheet. The exact assembly varies by roofing manufacturer and project specification.
Is torch-down roofing good for flat roofs?
Modified bitumen systems are widely used for flat and low-slope roofing applications. Whether torch application is appropriate depends on the particular building, roof conditions, safety requirements, code requirements, and manufacturer specifications.
What is modified bitumen roofing?
Modified bitumen is an asphalt-based roofing membrane modified with polymers and reinforced for use in roofing systems. APP and SBS are two common modified-bitumen technologies.
Why install three roofing layers?
A three-ply system provides multiple layers of waterproofing protection and redundancy rather than relying exclusively on one membrane.
What is the top layer of a torch-down roof?
The visible finished layer is commonly a granulated modified-bitumen cap sheet, depending on the selected roofing system.
Can a torch-down roof be installed over an existing roof?
Sometimes existing conditions allow an overlay system, but a complete roof evaluation is required. Existing roofing condition, number of layers, moisture, decking, code requirements, manufacturer specifications, and roof weight must all be considered.
What happens if rotten plywood is found?
Deteriorated decking should be addressed before installing the new roofing system so the membranes have a suitable substrate.
Can a torch-down roof fix ponding water?
Installing a new membrane does not automatically correct an existing slope or drainage problem. Significant ponding should be evaluated separately, and drainage or slope corrections may need to be included in the project scope.
Can skylights be replaced during a flat roof replacement?
Yes. Roof replacement is often a good time to replace aging skylights because the new skylight flashing and roofing system can be integrated together.
Does a torch-down roof need maintenance?
Yes. Drains should remain clear, and the roofing membrane, flashing, skylights, penetrations, and drainage areas should be inspected periodically.
How do I get an estimate for a 3-layer flat roof replacement?

Schedule a professional roof inspection with Roof Express. The existing roofing system, decking, drainage, flashing, penetrations, and access conditions can then be evaluated before a detailed proposal is prepared.

### Asphalt Shingle Reroofing Project in San Mateo, CA

Source: https://roof-ex.com/blog/field-notes/asphalt-shingle-reroofing-project-in-san-mateo-ca

Asphalt Shingle Reroofing Project in San Mateo, CA
A complete asphalt shingle reroofing project in San Mateo, California is about much more than replacing the shingles visible from the street.

A properly completed roof replacement starts with removing the aging roofing system, inspecting the roof deck, correcting damaged areas, installing new waterproofing and underlayment, properly flashing critical roof transitions, and finishing the project with a professionally installed architectural shingle roofing system.

At Roof Express, our goal is to build a complete roofing system designed to protect the home for years to come.

For this San Mateo reroofing project, the roofing process focuses on the entire assembly—from the plywood roof deck all the way to the finished shingles, ridge components, ventilation, and flashing details.
Why This San Mateo Home Needed a New Roof
Asphalt shingle roofs naturally deteriorate over time because of sun exposure, wind, rain, temperature changes, and normal aging.

Some of the warning signs that can indicate it is time for a reroof include:

Cracked or deteriorated shingles

Missing shingles

Curling shingle edges

Excessive granule loss

Exposed roofing nails

Deteriorated flashing

Previous roof patches

Recurring leaks

Water stains inside the home

Damaged roof decking

An aging roofing system nearing the end of its service life

When deterioration affects large portions of the roofing system, a complete reroof can provide a better long-term solution than continuing with isolated repairs.
Complete Tear-Off of the Existing Shingle Roof
The first major step in a professional reroofing project is removal of the existing roofing materials.

Depending on existing conditions, this may include removal of:

Existing asphalt shingles

Old roofing underlayment

Ridge materials

Roofing nails and fasteners

Deteriorated flashing

Damaged roofing accessories

Existing vents being replaced

Roofing debris

A complete tear-off gives the roofing contractor something that cannot be achieved through a simple overlay: direct access to the roof deck underneath.
Roof Deck Inspection After Tear-Off
Once the old roofing is removed, the roof decking can be properly inspected.

This is one of the most important stages of a roof replacement.

We evaluate exposed sheathing for conditions including:

Rotten plywood

Water damage

Delamination

Soft decking

Dry rot

Previous improper repairs

Damaged wood

Areas unsuitable for new roofing installation

The finished shingles may look perfect, but the roofing system is only as dependable as the structure supporting it.

Any deteriorated decking that needs replacement should be addressed before the new roofing system is installed.
Replacing Damaged Roof Decking
If deteriorated plywood is discovered during tear-off, affected sections are removed and replaced as required by the project scope.

New roofing should be installed over a solid, properly prepared surface.

Roof-deck replacement also provides an opportunity to correct old areas that may have been patched improperly during previous roofing work.

A detailed roofing contract should explain how concealed decking conditions are handled so homeowners understand the process before tear-off begins.
Installing New Roofing Underlayment
After the roof deck is prepared, the new roofing assembly begins.

High-quality roofing underlayment provides an additional protective layer between the wood roof deck and the asphalt shingles.

The complete assembly works together:

Roof Deck → Underlayment → Waterproofing → Flashing → Architectural Shingles → Ventilation → Drainage

The shingles may be the most visible part of the roof, but every layer underneath contributes to its long-term performance.
Additional Waterproofing at Critical Areas
Certain parts of a pitched roof experience greater water exposure than others.

Depending on the roof design, additional waterproofing protection may be installed around critical locations such as:

Roof valleys

Eaves

Skylights

Chimneys

Plumbing vents

Roof-to-wall connections

Other penetrations

These vulnerable areas deserve special attention because many roofing leaks originate around transitions rather than through the middle of the shingles.
Roof Valleys
Valleys collect rainwater from multiple roof surfaces.

Because a large amount of water can travel through these areas during a storm, proper valley preparation is essential.

A complete reroof should evaluate:

Existing valley conditions

Underlayment

Waterproofing

Metal components where applicable

Shingle installation

Drainage path

Properly constructed valleys help channel water safely toward the gutter system.

Once the roof deck, underlayment, and waterproofing details are ready, the new architectural asphalt shingles are installed.

Roof-to-wall transitions

Improper drainage

Damage

Downspout problems

The roofing system's job is to shed rainwater. The gutters and downspouts then need to move that water safely away from the structure.

The City's current building permit application specifically includes a reroof category and asks for information including the number of roofing squares, roofing material, and whether hot work is involved.

Project-specific requirements should always be confirmed before construction begins.

Not every roof needs complete replacement.

The roof is relatively new

Most shingles remain in good condition

Complete reroofing may make more sense when:

Shingles are deteriorated throughout

Leaks occur in multiple areas

Numerous repairs have already been completed

Roof decking has widespread problems

The roofing system is approaching the end of its expected service life

Repair expenses continue increasing

Asphalt Shingle Roof Replacement in San Bruno | Roof Express

Transforming Homes: A Complete Asphalt Shingle Roof Replacement in San Bruno
When it comes to protecting your most valuable asset, the roof over your head does all the heavy lifting. Recently, the expert crew at Roof Express had the privilege of completing a full asphalt shingle roof replacement for a beautiful home right here in San Bruno, California.

The homeowners were looking for a roofing solution that could withstand the unique microclimates of the Bay Area while simultaneously boosting their home's curb appeal and energy efficiency. We delivered exactly that.
In this comprehensive project spotlight, we are pulling back the curtain to show you exactly what goes into a professional roof replacement, why we selected premium materials, and how the right roofing contractor makes all the difference.

The San Bruno Roofing Challenge: Climate Matters
Living in San Bruno means enjoying beautiful coastal weather, but it also means your home is subjected to a unique set of environmental stressors.

 Coastal Moisture & Fog: The heavy morning fog rolling over the hills introduces constant moisture, which can accelerate wear and tear on inferior roofing materials.

Intense UV Exposure: During the summer, the relentless California sun beats down on your roof, breaking down the asphalt and driving up indoor temperatures.

 High Winds: The geography of the Peninsula often creates wind tunnels, making wind uplift a serious threat to loose or aging shingles.
To combat these local elements, a standard, run-of-the-mill roof simply will not cut it. You need a roofing system specifically engineered for the California climate.

The Solution: CertainTeed Landmark® PRO Solaris® Shingles
For this San Bruno project, the Roof Express team installed **CertainTeed Landmark PRO Solaris** asphalt shingles. As a top-rated roofing contractor, we have hands-on experience with nearly every material on the market, and this specific shingle line stands out as a premier choice for Bay Area homeowners.

Here is a deep dive into why we consistently recommend this product:

1. Superior Energy Efficiency (Title 24 Compliant)
California’s Title 24 energy standards are strict, and for good reason. The Solaris line features advanced **cool roof technology**. These shingles are manufactured with specially designed reflective granules that bounce solar energy back into the atmosphere rather than absorbing it into your attic.
 The Result: A significantly cooler home during the summer, less strain on your HVAC system, and noticeably lower monthly energy bills.

2. Maximum Durability and Weather Defense
The Landmark PRO series is built with a dual-layer, high-performance design that offers an extra-thick layer of weather protection.

 Impact Resistance:They are highly resistant to impact from falling branches or heavy hail.
 Wind Resistance: Engineered to stay put, these shingles carry an impressive wind resistance rating of up to 110 mph (and up to 130 mph with special installation upgrades).

 Fire Safety: They boast an Underwriters Laboratories (UL) Class A fire resistance rating, giving homeowners ultimate peace of mind.
3. Unmatched Architectural Curb Appeal
A new roof should be as beautiful as it is functional. The "Max Def" (Maximum Definition) color palette of the Landmark PRO series offers a richer mixture of surface granules. This creates a deeply dimensional, wood-shake look that instantly elevates the visual aesthetic and resale value of the property.

The Roof Express Installation Process: Step-by-Step
A premium shingle can only perform perfectly if it is installed perfectly. Our team at Roof Express follows a strict, quality-controlled process to ensure every project crosses the finish line with zero defects. Here is how we handled this San Bruno completion:

Phase 1: Comprehensive Inspection and Protection
Before a single shingle is removed, we protect the property. We strategically place tarps over landscaping, driveways, and patios to catch debris. We also conduct a final structural check to prepare for the tear-off.

Phase 2: The Tear-Off
We completely remove the old, failing roof down to the bare wooden decking. Learn more about roof tear-off and replacement: https://roof-ex.com/roof-replacement. We never recommend "roof-overs" (installing new shingles over old ones), as this hides underlying rot and voids manufacturer warranties.

Phase 3: Deck Prep and Underlayment
Once the decking is exposed, we inspect every square inch for wood rot or water damage, replacing any compromised boards. Next, we install a high-quality, synthetic underlayment. This acts as a secondary, waterproof barrier between the wood deck and the new shingles. We also install heavy-duty ice and water shields in the roof valleys and around penetrations (like vents and chimneys).

Phase 4: Precision Shingle Installation
This is where the Roof Express crew truly shines. Using chalk lines for laser-straight rows, we install the CertainTeed Landmark PRO Solaris shingles using a specialized nailing pattern. Every nail is driven flush and positioned perfectly on the nail line to ensure maximum wind resistance.

Phase 5: Ventilation and Flashing
A roof must breathe to last. We install brand-new, customized flashing around all roof penetrations to prevent leaks. We also upgrade the attic ventilation systems (ridge vents and soffit vents) to ensure proper airflow, which prevents moisture buildup and prolongs the life of the new shingles.

Phase 6: The Final Cleanup
We believe we should leave your property looking better than we found it. We use heavy-duty magnetic sweepers across your entire yard and driveway to pick up any stray nails, ensuring a safe environment for your family and pets.

Asphalt Shingle Roof Replacement in San Francisco

San Francisco homeowners frequently choose asphalt shingle roofing systems because they offer durability, affordability, and excellent weather resistance for the Bay Area climate. Whether a roof has reached the end of its life or has sustained storm damage, a professional asphalt shingle roof replacement ensures the home remains protected from moisture, wind, and structural deterioration.

At ROOF EXPRESS, replacing aging roofs with high-performance asphalt shingles is one of the most common projects completed across San Francisco neighborhoods. From Sunset District homes exposed to coastal fog to properties in Noe Valley and Pacific Heights facing wind-driven rain, a properly installed asphalt roof system can last 25–35 years when built with the right materials and installation methods.

Why Asphalt Shingle Roofs Are Popular in San Francisco

Asphalt shingles are the most widely installed roofing material in the United States, and they are especially suitable for San Francisco’s climate. Their layered composition provides strong protection against wind, moisture, and UV exposure while maintaining a clean architectural appearance that complements many Bay Area homes.

Modern architectural shingles such as GAF Timberline HDZ, CertainTeed Landmark PRO, and Owens Corning Duration are designed with advanced adhesive strips and algae-resistant granules. These features improve wind resistance and help maintain the roof’s color and durability over time.

For many San Francisco homeowners, asphalt shingles provide the perfect balance between performance, longevity, and cost efficiency.

The Asphalt Shingle Roof Replacement Process

A professional asphalt shingle roof replacement follows a structured installation process to ensure long-term performance and compliance with California building codes.

Roof Inspection and Permit Process

The project typically begins with a detailed inspection to evaluate the roof structure, ventilation, and decking condition. In San Francisco, most full roof replacements require a permit to ensure that the work meets safety and structural standards.

Tear-Off of the Existing Roof

Old roofing materials are carefully removed down to the roof deck. This step is critical because it allows contractors to inspect the underlying plywood or plank decking and replace any damaged sections.

Roof Deck Preparation

Once exposed, the roof deck is reinforced where necessary. New plywood or OSB sheathing may be installed to create a stable surface for the new roofing system.

Waterproof Underlayment Installation

High-quality underlayment is applied to protect the structure from water infiltration. Many professional installations include synthetic underlayment and ice & water barrier membranes in vulnerable areas such as valleys, eaves, and around penetrations.

Shingle Installation

Architectural asphalt shingles are installed in overlapping layers to create a waterproof barrier. Starter shingles, ridge caps, and proper nailing patterns are essential to ensure wind resistance and long-term durability.

Ventilation and Final Inspection

Proper attic ventilation is crucial for maintaining roof health. Ridge vents, intake vents, or other ventilation solutions help regulate temperature and prevent moisture buildup inside the attic.

Benefits of Installing a New Asphalt Shingle Roof

A professionally installed asphalt shingle roof offers several important advantages for homeowners in San Francisco.

First, it improves weather resistance, protecting the home from rain, fog, and coastal wind conditions common throughout the Bay Area.

Second, it increases property value and curb appeal. New architectural shingles provide a clean and modern appearance that enhances the overall look of the home.

Third, modern asphalt shingles are engineered for energy efficiency and durability, helping reduce long-term maintenance costs.

When Should a San Francisco Homeowner Replace Their Roof?

Many roofs in San Francisco begin showing signs of aging after 20–30 years. Homeowners should consider replacement if they notice:

• Curling or missing shingles

• Granule loss or dark streaks

• Persistent roof leaks

• Sagging or damaged decking

• Storm or wind damage

Addressing these issues early can prevent costly structural damage to the home.

Choosing the Right Roofing Contractor in San Francisco

Roof replacement is a major investment, so selecting a qualified contractor is essential. Homeowners should work with licensed, insured roofing professionals who follow California building codes and use high-quality materials from reputable manufacturers.

A trusted roofing company will also provide clear project timelines, warranty coverage, and transparent communication throughout the installation process.

Roof Repair or Complete Roof Replacement?
One of the most common questions homeowners ask is whether they should repair or replace their roof.

A repair may make sense when the roofing system is generally in good condition and the problem is isolated.

For example, a localized leak around a penetration or a small damaged section may be repairable.

Complete roof replacement may be more appropriate when:

The roof has widespread deterioration

Several areas are leaking

Roofing materials are reaching the end of their expected life

Large portions of the roof have already been repaired

The waterproofing system has deteriorated

The homeowner wants a complete long-term roofing solution

Roof Express can inspect the roof and explain the available options so the property owner can make an informed decision.

### Chimney Leak Repair in Daly City (2026 Guide)

Source: https://roof-ex.com/blog/field-notes/chimney-leak-repair-in-daly-city-2026-guide

Chimney Leak Repair in Daly City (2026 Guide)
Why Chimney Leaks Happen & Why Fast Repair Is Critical

Chimney leaks are one of the most common roofing problems in Daly City. With strong coastal winds, frequent fog, and heavy winter rain, chimneys are highly exposed to moisture. If flashing or masonry fails, water can quickly enter your attic, ceilings, and walls.

Timely chimney leak repair protects your roof structure, prevents mold growth, and avoids costly interior damage.

Why Chimney Leaks Are Common in Daly City

4

Homes in Daly City experience:

🌫 Constant marine moisture

🌧 Heavy winter storms

💨 Strong wind-driven rain

🏘 Aging flashing systems

🧱 Brick and mortar deterioration

Because chimneys interrupt the roof surface, they require precise waterproofing to prevent leaks.

Common Causes of Chimney Leaks
1️⃣ Damaged or Improper Flashing

Flashing seals the gap between the chimney and roof. If it lifts, cracks, or rusts, water enters immediately.

2️⃣ Cracked Mortar or Masonry

Over time, brick chimneys absorb moisture. Cracked mortar joints allow water to penetrate.

3️⃣ Worn Chimney Cap

A damaged or missing chimney cap allows rainwater to flow directly into the flue.

4️⃣ Missing Ice & Water Barrier

Improper underlayment around the chimney base increases leak risk.

5️⃣ Sealant Failure

Old caulking dries and cracks, breaking the waterproof seal.

Signs Your Chimney Is Leaking

Water stains near fireplace walls

Ceiling stains near chimney area

Musty attic smell

Dripping during rain

Rusted flashing

Peeling paint near chimney

Leaks may appear far from the actual chimney location due to water traveling along framing.

Professional Chimney Leak Repair Process

### Common Flat Roof Drain Problems in San Francisco (And How to Fix Them)

Common Flat Roof Drain Problems in San Francisco (And How to Fix Them)

San Francisco’s mix of coastal fog, salty air, wind-driven rain, and aging buildings makes flat roof drainage a serious concern for property owners. At Roof Express, we’ve seen firsthand how small drainage issues can turn into expensive structural damage if ignored.

Here’s what you need to know about the most common flat roof drain problems in San Francisco—and how to prevent them.

1. Ponding Water After Rainstorms

Ponding water is one of the most frequent flat roof issues in San Francisco. Even though our rainy season is shorter than other regions, when it rains, it can come down hard.

Why it happens:

Improper roof slope

Clogged drains

Settling or sagging roof deck

Blocked scuppers

Why it’s a problem:

Accelerates membrane deterioration

Leads to leaks and interior water damage

Increases structural load on older buildings

Solution: Routine inspections before and during the rainy season ensure drains are clear and slopes are functioning properly.

2. Clogged Roof Drains & Scuppers

San Francisco’s urban debris—leaves, trash, and even bird nesting materials—can quickly clog drainage systems.

Warning signs:

Water overflowing edges

Slow drainage during rain

Debris buildup around drain openings

Common causes in SF:

Wind-blown debris

Nearby trees

Aging drain strainers

Lack of seasonal maintenance

Solution: Preventative maintenance and professional drain cleaning twice a year (especially before winter).

3. Corroded or Rusted Drain Components

San Francisco’s proximity to the Pacific Ocean means salt air exposure—especially in neighborhoods like the Sunset and Richmond.

What happens:

Metal drain bowls rust

Fasteners deteriorate

Drain pipes weaken and leak

Solution: Replace older metal components with corrosion-resistant materials such as PVC or coated metals.

4. Improperly Installed Internal Drains

Many older San Francisco buildings have legacy roofing systems. Poor flashing or improper drain installation often leads to hidden leaks.

Signs of trouble:

Ceiling stains

Bubbling membrane near drains

Recurring leaks despite patchwork repairs

Solution: Professional evaluation of flashing and drain integration. In many cases, re-flashing or upgrading the drain assembly is required.

5. Collapsed or Blocked Downspouts

Sometimes the problem isn’t on the roof—it’s in the vertical drainage system.

Causes:

Old cast iron piping

Tree root intrusion

Debris compaction

Structural shifting in older buildings

Solution: Camera inspections and pipe clearing to ensure the entire drainage system is functioning.

Why Flat Roof Drainage Matters in San Francisco

Flat roofs are common across SF’s commercial buildings, multi-family properties, and mixed-use structures. Because many buildings are older, drainage systems are often past their lifespan.

Unchecked drainage issues can lead to:

Interior mold growth

Structural rot

Electrical hazards

Expensive emergency repairs

Preventative maintenance costs far less than water damage restoration.

Step-by-Step: How Roof Express Finishes a Shingle Roof

   Open metal valleys or properly woven closed valleys are sealed and flashed to handle heavy rainwater runoff. Step flashing around chimneys, skylights, vents, and walls is woven seamlessly with the shingles.    Specialized ridge cap shingles (often matching your architectural shingles) are installed along the peaks and hips. These provide ventilation, a clean finished look, and superior wind resistance. Proper overlap and nailing here are critical for long-term performance.

   Overhanging shingles slightly at the eaves directs water cleanly into gutters. We ensure consistent exposure (typically 5–5.5 inches) across every course for a uniform, professional appearance.

   Our crews perform multiple checkpoints, verifying nail placement in the reinforced nailing zone, proper adhesive sealing, and overall system integrity. We coordinate with Walnut Creek building inspectors for final approval and handle all permitting and documentation.

   Every job ends with a complete site cleanup, including magnetic sweeps to remove stray nails from your lawn, driveway, and landscaping. Your property is left spotless.

### El Niño in San Francisco & the Bay Area

Source: https://roof-ex.com/blog/field-notes/el-ni-o-in-san-francisco-the-bay-area

El Niño in San Francisco & the Bay Area

How Homeowners Can Prepare Their Roof Before Heavy Rain

By Roof Express | San Francisco Bay Area Roofing Professionals

El Niño can bring periods of heavier-than-normal rainfall and powerful Pacific storm systems to California. For homeowners in San Francisco and throughout the Bay Area, prolonged rain can expose roofing problems that may have gone unnoticed during the dry season.

A roof may look perfectly fine from the ground but still have aging flashing, deteriorated sealant, clogged drainage, loose shingles, or small openings around penetrations. Once several days of rain arrive, these minor vulnerabilities can turn into interior leaks and water damage.

Preparing before the rainy season is usually much easier than discovering a roofing problem during a major storm.

What Is El Niño?

El Niño is a climate pattern associated with unusually warm surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean. It can influence weather patterns around the world.

For California, El Niño does not guarantee that every location will experience extreme rainfall. However, some El Niño winters have been associated with wetter conditions and significant storms in parts of the state.

For Bay Area homeowners, the practical lesson is simple: regardless of the seasonal forecast, your roof and drainage system should be ready before extended periods of winter rain.

Why Bay Area Roofs Can Be Vulnerable During Heavy Rain

San Francisco and surrounding Bay Area communities contain a wide variety of roofing systems, including asphalt shingles, modified-bitumen low-slope roofs, tile roofs, older built-up roofing systems, skylights, roof decks, and combinations of pitched and flat roofing.

During prolonged rainfall, water can find vulnerabilities around:

Skylights and their flashing

Plumbing vents and pipe penetrations

Chimneys

Roof-to-wall transitions

Valleys

Missing, loose, cracked, or deteriorated shingles

Aging low-slope roofing seams

Roof drains and scuppers

Gutters and downspouts

Previously repaired roofing areas

One short rainstorm may not reveal a problem. Several consecutive days of wind-driven rain can be a very different test.

8 Things Homeowners Should Do Before El Niño or the Rainy Season

1. Schedule a professional roof inspection. Have the roof checked before major storms arrive. An inspection can identify visible deterioration, damaged shingles, questionable flashing, drainage problems, and other areas that may require maintenance.

2. Clean gutters and downspouts. Leaves and debris can restrict drainage. When gutters overflow, water can reach fascia boards, siding, windows, foundations, and other areas where it shouldn’t go.

3. Inspect skylights and roof penetrations. Skylights, plumbing vents, exhaust vents, chimneys, and other penetrations deserve particular attention because they interrupt the continuous roofing surface.

4. Check flat and low-slope roof drainage. Standing water can place additional stress on a roofing system. Roof drains, scuppers, and drainage paths should be clear before heavy rainfall.

5. Address small roofing problems early. A loose shingle, deteriorated flashing detail, or compromised roof penetration may be relatively manageable during dry weather. Waiting until water is entering the building can make the situation considerably more complicated.

6. Trim problematic vegetation. Tree limbs hanging over a roof can drop leaves into gutters and drains, rub against roofing materials, or become a hazard during strong winds. Tree work should be performed safely by an appropriate professional.

7. Look inside the attic when accessible. Signs such as staining, damp wood, deteriorated sheathing, or previous water marks can indicate that the roof should receive closer attention. Do not enter unsafe or difficult-to-access attic areas.

8. Document your roof’s condition. Photos taken before storm season can be useful for maintenance records and for comparing conditions after severe weather.

What Should You Do During an El Niño Storm?

Safety comes first. Homeowners should not climb onto a wet roof during rain or high winds.

If you notice a leak, place a container underneath dripping water when it is safe to do so and move furniture, electronics, and valuables away from the affected area. Photograph visible water damage and note when and where the leak occurred.

If water is near electrical fixtures, outlets, or wiring, avoid contact with the affected area and seek appropriate professional assistance.

Contact a roofing professional to discuss the leak, but understand that certain repairs may need to wait until conditions are safe enough for technicians to access the roof.

Watch for These Warning Signs After Heavy Rain

Once the storm has passed, inspect your property from a safe location. Pay attention to ceiling stains, bubbling paint, damp walls, musty odors, missing shingles, overflowing gutters, damaged flashing, or unexplained moisture in the attic.

A leak may also appear some distance from the actual roof opening. Water can travel along roof decking, framing, pipes, or other building components before becoming visible inside the home. That is one reason accurately diagnosing a roof leak can require a professional inspection.

Don’t Wait for the First Major Storm

Roofing contractors often become much busier once widespread rain begins. Emergency calls increase, working conditions become more difficult, and some repairs cannot safely be completed while a storm is underway.

The best time to prepare is while the roof is dry.

Preventive maintenance cannot guarantee that a home will never experience storm damage, but identifying existing roofing and drainage problems before prolonged rainfall can substantially reduce avoidable risks.

Preparing San Francisco Bay Area Homes for Rain

Roof Express provides roofing inspections, maintenance, repairs, and roof replacement services throughout San Francisco and surrounding Bay Area communities.

Our team works with asphalt shingle roofs, low-slope roofing systems, skylights, gutters, roof penetrations, flashing, and other common residential roofing components.

If your roof hasn’t been inspected recently—or you’ve noticed previous leaks, aging roofing materials, damaged shingles, or drainage problems—consider having it evaluated before the next major series of storms.

### Fighting the Fog: The Best Roofing Materials for Daly City Coastal Homes

Source: https://roof-ex.com/blog/field-notes/fighting-the-fog-the-best-roofing-materials-for-daly-city-coastal-homes

Fighting the Fog: The Best Roofing Materials for Daly City Coastal Homes

Daly City homeowners know the unique, cool beauty of our coastal fog rolling over the hills. However, they also know that what works on a roof in San Bruno or even other parts of the Bay Area won't survive long here. Our persistent moisture, frequent fog cycles, and gusty winds place incredible stress on standard roofing.

When it’s time to repair or replace, choosing the right material isn't just about color; it's about engineering. To help you make the best, most search-intent decision, Roof Express has compiled this guide to the specific marine-grade and algae-resistant materials designed to withstand Daly City's environment.

Why Material Choice Matters in the 'Fog Belt'

Standard architectural shingles might look great, but without specific features, they can fail prematurely in our microclimate.

• Black Stalks/Algae Growth: Have you ever noticed black streaks or moss on a neighbor's roof? That's gloeocapsa magma (a type of cyanobacteria) that thrives in our constant dampness. It isn't just cosmetic; it eats away at shingle granules and traps moisture, accelerating rot.

• Moisture-Induced Leaks: Our fog cycles constantly introduce moisture, which can penetrate small gaps or saturate underlayments.

• Corrosion of Components: Salt-laden coastal air accelerates the corrosion of standard metal flashing, fasteners, and gutter components.

• Wind and Shingle Uplift: Our coastal position means significant, consistent winds that can lift and damage un-strengthened materials.

Top Coastal Roofing Materials: Engineered for Daly City

Use these search-intent material types as your guide. They address the precise challenges we face.

1. Marine-Grade Synthetic Underlayment

Don't settle for basic roofing felt. High-performance, marine-grade synthetic underlayment provides an essential, primary water barrier that is far superior at preventing moisture infiltration from our constant fog. It is tear-resistant and protects against the damage caused by relentless dampness. (Keywords: synthetic underlayment, marine-grade roof protection).

2. High-Algae-Resistant Composite Shingles

Demand shingles specifically engineered with advanced copper granules and a powerful, long-lasting algae-resistant technology (often designated as AR). These composites prevent those ugly black streaks (Gloeocapsa magma) from ever forming, keeping your roof clean and protected. 

3. Wind-Strengthened High-Wind Architectural Shingles

Our coastal winds are no joke. Look for architectural shingles that carry a specialized, high-wind speed rating (often tested to 130+ MPH) and feature an enhanced sealant bond. This ensures they resist uplift and stay secure during our storms.

4. Corrosion-Resistant Metal Flashing and Fasteners

(Pictured as specialized coated metal sample).

This is where standard solutions fail most. Insist on flashing (e.g., drip edge, valley, and chimney) and fasteners made from corrosion-resistant materials. In Daly City, that means using aluminum with specialized coatings, specific types of high-grade stainless steel, or even zinc-coated steel, but never basic galvanized steel, which corrodes quickly in our salty air. 

Signs of Coastal-Specific Roof Damage (Search-Intent Alert)

While general damage is easy to spot, keep an eye out for these localized signs:

• Dark Streaks (Algae/Cyanobacteria): This is the clearest sign your roof lacks the required algae resistance. 

• Corroded Metal Components: Check your flashing, drip edge, and gutters for rust or pitting. 

• Premature Shingle Granule Loss: If your shingles look bald early, it might be due to moisture and algae damage. 

Final Thought: Specialized Expertise with Roof Express

When you see the Roof Express badge (featured as a durable metal field emblem and business cards), you are choosing a team that understands these exact materials and how to install them properly for the Daly City climate. We don't just "do roofs"; we provide specialized, marine-grade defense for your biggest asset.

Ready to invest in a roof that can handle the fog? Contact Roof Express for a free, localized material consultation and inspection. We'll help you build for longevity on the coast. Call (650) 666 5554... to secure your home.

### Flat Roof Project Completed in San Francisco: Torch-Down

Source: https://roof-ex.com/blog/field-notes/flat-roof-project-completed-in-san-francisco-torch-down

Flat Roof Project Completed in San Francisco: Torch-Down Installation, Timeline, Cost Factors & Maintenance Tips (2026 Guide)

A flat roof project in San Francisco isn’t just a “replace and forget” job. Between coastal fog, wind-driven rain, UV exposure, and older building conditions, a properly completed flat roof needs the right system, the right details, and clean workmanship from start to finish.

In this blog, we’ll walk through what a completed flat roof project in San Francisco looks like—step by step—so homeowners and property managers understand the process, what affects price, how long it takes, and how to protect the roof for the long run.

Quick Summary of the Flat Roof Completion (San Francisco)

A completed flat roof project typically includes:

Tear-off of old roofing (if needed) and proper debris disposal

Deck inspection and repairs (dry rot / damaged plywood replacement)

New base sheet + cap sheet installation (commonly torch-down modified bitumen)

New flashings at all walls, skylights, vents, and parapets

Drainage corrections (scuppers, internal drains, crickets/saddles)

Final waterproofing checks and clean finish details

This is how you get a flat roof that performs in San Francisco conditions—especially during winter storms.

Why Flat Roofs in San Francisco Need Special Attention

San Francisco has unique conditions that impact flat roofing performance:

Moisture exposure: fog, marine layer, and damp mornings

Wind: stronger gusts can lift poorly sealed edges and flashings

Older structures: many buildings have aging roof decks and parapet walls

Drainage challenges: flat roofs must move water efficiently to drains/scuppers

Because of this, the biggest failures we see are not the field membrane—it’s the details (edges, flashings, terminations, and drainage).

Completed Flat Roof System Used Most Often: Torch-Down Modified Bitumen

One of the most common high-performing flat roof systems in San Francisco is modified bitumen torch-down (often installed as a 2-ply system):

1) Base Sheet (Foundation Layer)

Mechanically fastened or adhered to the deck

Creates stability and separation from the substrate

2) Cap Sheet (Top Waterproof Layer)

Heat-welded (torch-applied) to create sealed overlaps

Granulated surface protects against UV and weather

Why it’s popular in SF: It’s durable, repairable, and handles fluctuating moisture conditions well when installed correctly.

Flat Roof Project Completion: Step-by-Step Process
1) Site Protection + Setup

Before work begins, the crew protects:

walkways, landscaping, and siding

neighbor-sensitive areas (tight property lines are common in SF)

attic/indoor spaces from debris and dust (where applicable)

2) Tear-Off (If Needed)

If the roof has:

multiple layers,

trapped moisture,

brittle cracking,

or poor prior workmanship,

a full removal is often the best long-term choice. After tear-off, we inspect the deck closely.

3) Deck Inspection + Plywood Replacement

This is a critical part of a “completion” done right.

Common findings in SF:

soft spots near drains/scuppers

dry rot at parapet walls

damaged decking around vent penetrations

Any compromised sheathing gets replaced so the new system isn’t installed over weak structure.

4) Underlayment / Base Sheet Installation

Base sheet is installed with correct attachment and alignment, ensuring:

straight overlaps

proper fastening patterns

a smooth surface (no bubbles or ridges)

5) Cap Sheet Torch-Down Installation

This is where skill matters.

A proper torch-down finish includes:

fully sealed laps (no voids)

consistent heat-welding

clean edges and terminations

reinforced areas at transitions

6) Flashings & Waterproof Details (The “Make or Break” Stage)

The roof field can look perfect—but flashings are what stop leaks.

Completed projects typically include:

wall-to-roof transitions

parapet cap or termination bar installs

vent pipe flashings

skylight curbs properly sealed

counterflashing where required

7) Drainage Improvements

Standing water destroys flat roofs early.

A quality completion addresses:

slope corrections (tapered build-up where needed)

crickets behind chimneys or large curbs

scupper rework or drain upgrades

ensuring clean, open water paths

8) Final Walkthrough + Cleanup

A completed flat roof job should finish with:

magnet sweep for nails and fasteners

clean perimeter edges

photo documentation (great for warranty + insurance records)

maintenance recommendations

### Flat Roof Ready for Solar Installation

Source: https://roof-ex.com/blog/field-notes/flat-roof-ready-for-solar-installation

Flat Roof Ready for Solar Installation

Why Roofing Should Come First
Installing solar panels is a major investment, but before mounting a new solar system on a flat roof, homeowners should make sure the roofing system underneath is ready.

A solar installation can remain on a roof for many years. If the roof begins leaking or needs replacement shortly after the solar panels are installed, the panels may need to be removed and reinstalled before the roofing work can be completed.

That can create additional cost, scheduling delays, and unnecessary disruption.

This is why it is often better to inspect, repair, or replace an aging flat roof before solar installation begins.

At Roof Express, we help homeowners prepare flat and low-slope roofs for future solar installation by addressing waterproofing, roof decking, drainage, flashing, penetrations, and other roofing conditions before solar equipment is mounted.
Why the Roof Should Be Evaluated Before Solar Installation
Solar panels do not replace your roofing system.

They are installed above it.

The roof underneath still needs to provide dependable waterproof protection for the building.

Before solar installation, the roof should be evaluated for:

Existing leaks

Open seams

Cracked roofing membranes

Blisters or bubbles

Ponding water

Damaged flashing

Soft roof decking

Deteriorated drains

Previous temporary repairs

Failed roof-to-wall transitions

Aging roofing materials

If the roofing system is already approaching the end of its useful life, replacing it before solar installation may be the better long-term decision.
Why Replacing the Roof After Solar Can Be More Complicated
Once solar panels and mounting equipment are installed, access to the roofing system becomes more difficult.

If the roof later needs major repairs or replacement, the project may involve:

Disconnecting the solar system

Removing the solar panels

Removing or modifying mounting equipment

Completing the roofing work

Reinstalling the solar equipment

Reconnecting and testing the solar system

This can add additional labor and coordination to a project that could have been avoided by addressing the roof first.
Flat Roof Replacement Before Solar Installation
When an existing flat roof is aging or deteriorated, a complete replacement before solar installation creates a fresh roofing foundation.

The process may include:

Removing the existing roofing

Inspecting the roof deck

Replacing deteriorated plywood

Evaluating drainage

Installing a new roofing assembly

Rebuilding flashing details

Waterproofing roof penetrations

Completing the finished roof

Allowing the solar contractor to install equipment over the new system

This provides the solar installer with a new and properly prepared roofing surface.
Modified Bitumen Roofing for Solar-Ready Flat Roofs
Modified bitumen is one of the roofing systems commonly used for flat and low-slope roofs.

For appropriate properties, a multi-layer modified bitumen roofing assembly can provide a strong waterproofing foundation before solar installation.

A typical 3-layer system may include:

Layer 1 — Base Sheet

Layer 2 — Modified Bitumen Interply

Layer 3 — Granulated Modified Bitumen Cap Sheet

Each layer adds protection to the complete roofing assembly.

A new multi-ply roofing system can be especially valuable before solar equipment is installed because future access to some roof areas may become limited.
Roof Deck Inspection Before Solar
The roof deck is one of the most important parts of the roofing system.

Unfortunately, homeowners often cannot see the condition of the plywood underneath an existing roof.

During a complete tear-off, the roof deck can be inspected for:

Rotten plywood

Water damage

Delamination

Dry rot

Soft areas

Previous improper repairs

Structural deterioration

Solar mounting equipment should not be installed without considering the condition of the underlying roof structure.

Any damaged decking should be addressed before the new roofing and solar systems are installed.
Flat Roof Drainage and Solar Panels
Drainage should also be evaluated before solar installation.

Solar panels, racking, conduit, and other equipment can make future maintenance around drains more difficult.

The roof should be designed so water can continue moving toward:

Roof drains

Scuppers

Gutters

Downspouts

Existing ponding areas should be identified before the solar installation begins.

Installing solar panels over a roof with a major drainage problem does not correct the underlying condition.

When appropriate, drainage improvements may involve:

Tapered materials

Crickets

Slope improvements

Drain modifications

New sheathing

Scupper improvements

Keep Roof Drains Accessible
One important consideration when planning solar equipment is maintaining access to roof drains and scuppers.

Solar panels should not create unnecessary obstructions around critical drainage areas.

Homeowners should be able to inspect and clean these locations after installation.

Blocked drainage can lead to standing water and unnecessary stress on the roofing system.

Coordination between the roofing contractor and solar contractor can help avoid these problems.
Solar Mounting Penetrations Must Be Waterproofed
Depending on the solar mounting system, the installation may create penetrations through the roofing assembly.

Every penetration is a potential leak location if it is not properly waterproofed.

Solar mounting areas may require careful coordination between:

The solar contractor

The roofing contractor

The equipment manufacturer

Roof penetrations should be properly flashed and integrated into the roofing system rather than relying only on surface sealant.
Avoid Unnecessary Roof Penetrations
Whenever possible, the solar layout should minimize unnecessary penetrations through the roofing membrane.

The exact mounting system depends on the roof, structural requirements, solar equipment, and engineering specifications.

Some systems may use penetrations while others may use different mounting approaches.

Regardless of the system, the roofing contractor should understand where equipment will be installed so waterproofing concerns can be addressed before final installation.
Protecting a New Roof During Solar Installation
A newly installed flat roof can be damaged if other contractors are not careful while working on it.

Potential problems include:

Dropped tools

Sharp equipment

Dragging solar panels

Excessive foot traffic

Cutting the membrane

Improperly placed mounting equipment

New penetrations

Damage around roof edges

Solar installers should use appropriate protection when working over a new roofing membrane.

After solar installation, it can also be beneficial to have the roof inspected for accidental damage.
Roofing Warranty and Solar Installation
Homeowners should discuss roofing warranties before solar equipment is installed.

Some roofing warranties may contain requirements related to:

New roof penetrations

Third-party work

Modifications to the roofing system

Solar mounting systems

Flashing

Repairs

Before solar installation, ask your roofing contractor whether any additional steps are necessary to protect the roofing workmanship or manufacturer warranty.
Solar Panels and Future Roof Maintenance
Even after solar panels are installed, the roof still needs periodic maintenance.

Flat roof maintenance may include:

Cleaning drains

Removing debris

Inspecting flashing

Checking roof penetrations

Monitoring seams

Inspecting skylights

Checking parapet walls

Looking for membrane damage

Monitoring areas beneath or around solar equipment

Solar equipment should be positioned so important roofing components remain reasonably accessible whenever practical.
Skylights and Solar Planning
Many flat roofs contain skylights.

Solar panels should be planned carefully around skylights to maintain appropriate access and avoid interfering with:

Skylight flashing

Drainage

Future replacement

Maintenance

Emergency access where applicable

If an older skylight is already deteriorated, replacing it before the solar equipment is installed may prevent additional work later.

Many flat roofs also contain parapet walls.

These areas often contain important waterproofing transitions.

Deteriorated wall flashing

If the existing roofing system remains in good condition, repairs may be sufficient.

Repair work before solar may include:

The decision should be based on the overall condition of the roofing system, not just one visible problem.

Solar panel locations

Mounting locations

Areas requiring protection

Can solar panels damage a flat roof?

### Flat Roof Repair: 9 Warning Signs, Best Fixes,

Source: https://roof-ex.com/blog/field-notes/flat-roof-repair-9-warning-signs-best-fixes

Flat Roof Repair: 9 Warning Signs, Best Fixes, and How to Make a Flat Roof Last Longer

Flat roofs are popular for commercial buildings and many modern homes because they’re efficient and space-saving—but they require the right maintenance. When problems show up, they can escalate quickly because water drains more slowly than on a steep-slope roof.

This guide covers the most common flat roof issues, how repairs work, and what you can do to extend your roof’s life.

Why Flat Roofs Fail (Most Common Causes)

Most flat roof problems come from a few repeat issues:

Ponding water (water sits longer than it should)

Cracked seams or failed adhesive

Damaged flashing around edges, walls, skylights, and vents

UV exposure drying and shrinking materials

Poor drainage design or clogged drains/scuppers

Foot traffic or equipment damage (especially on commercial roofs)

9 Warning Signs Your Flat Roof Needs Repair
1) Ponding water that lasts more than 48 hours

Some standing water is common after heavy rain, but if it remains for days, it can weaken seams and accelerate membrane breakdown.

2) Bubbling, blistering, or “soft” areas

Bubbles often mean moisture trapped under the membrane. If not addressed, it can spread and lead to leaks.

3) Cracks, splits, or exposed seams

Flat roof systems rely heavily on seams. Even small gaps can let water in.

4) Leaks or water stains inside

Ceiling stains, damp insulation, or dripping after storms should trigger a quick inspection—flat roof leaks can travel far from the entry point.

5) Lifting edges or loose perimeter metal

Edge details take the most wind stress. Once edges lift, water infiltration becomes much easier.

6) Flashing damage around penetrations

Skylights, HVAC units, vents, and parapet walls are prime leak zones. If the flashing fails, the membrane can still be fine and you’ll still leak.

7) Moldy attic smell or increased humidity

Moisture can build up without obvious dripping. Odors and humidity changes can be early warning signs.

8) Granule loss (for modified bitumen) or membrane thinning

If your roof has a granulated surface, heavy granule loss exposes the membrane to UV damage and premature aging.

9) Visible punctures or wear paths

Walkways, rooftop equipment service, and fallen branches can puncture membranes.

Flat Roof Types (and How Repairs Differ)
TPO (Thermoplastic Polyolefin)

Common on commercial roofs

Repairs often involve heat-welded patches and seam reinforcement

Key failure points: seams, flashing, punctures

EPDM (Rubber Membrane)

Flexible and durable

Repairs often use primer + seam tape/patches

Key failure points: seams, adhesive failure, punctures

Modified Bitumen (Mod-Bit)

Asphalt-based with reinforcement

Repairs may use torch-down, cold-applied patch, or cap sheet repairs

Key failure points: splits, blisters, granule loss, flashing

Built-Up Roofing (BUR)

Multiple layers with gravel surface

Repairs may require cut-out and rebuild of damaged sections

Key failure points: cracks, surface wear, trapped moisture

Best Flat Roof Repair Options
Spot patch repair (best for punctures and small areas)

Great when damage is localized

Fast and affordable

Must be compatible with your roof system

Seam reinforcement (best for recurring seam issues)

Adds strength to high-risk seams

Works well for TPO/EPDM when caught early

Flashing rebuild (best for leaks around edges and penetrations)

One of the most effective long-term fixes

Especially important around skylights, parapet walls, and HVAC curbs

Drainage improvement (best for ponding water)

Cleaning drains is step one

If ponding is structural, solutions can include:

Adding tapered insulation

Installing additional drains/scuppers

Reworking crickets around rooftop units

Section replacement (best when the membrane is failing in one zone)

If moisture is widespread in one area, replacing a section can prevent repeated repairs

Repair vs. Replace: When Is a Flat Roof “Too Far Gone”?

Repair is usually a good choice when:

The roof is relatively young (often under ~10–15 years depending on material)

Problems are limited to seams, flashing, or punctures

Insulation and decking are dry and structurally sound

Replacement is often the better value when:

Leaks are recurring in multiple locations

Moisture is trapped beneath large areas of membrane

The membrane is shrinking, cracking, or heavily deteriorated

You have chronic ponding and the design needs correction

How to Make a Flat Roof Last Longer (Simple Maintenance Plan)

A little maintenance makes a big difference on flat roofs:

Monthly / after storms

Clear leaves and debris from drains and scuppers

Check for new punctures or lifted edges

Twice a year

Schedule a professional inspection (spring/fall is ideal)

Reseal minor flashing gaps before they become leaks

Anytime rooftop work happens

Protect the membrane during HVAC/solar/service work

Use walkway pads or designated paths for foot traffic

FAQs About Flat Roof Repair
How long does a flat roof repair last?

A properly done repair can last years, but it depends on the roof’s overall condition and whether the leak source was correctly identified.

Can I patch a flat roof myself?

Small temporary patches are possible, but flat roof systems require the right materials and methods (heat-weld, seam tape, compatible adhesives). Poor patches can trap moisture and cause bigger failures.

What’s the most common flat roof leak point?

Flashing and penetrations (vents, skylights, parapet walls) are the most common sources, followed by seams and punctures.

Is ponding water always a problem?

Not always—but if it lasts more than 48 hours regularly, it increases wear and can shorten the roof’s lifespan.

Call to Action

If you’re seeing any of the warning signs above, the safest move is a flat roof inspection. A qualified roofer can confirm:

The roof type and condition

Where water is entering (and how far it’s traveling)

Whether repairs will hold—or replacement is the smarter investment

If you’re in the San Francisco area, Roof Express is a strong local choice for inspections and flat roof repair/replacement.
